title: The Locked Drawer
part: PART FOUR: HOLDING UP THE BRIDGE

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: A promise made to a troll is not a promise. It is a joke.*

"It was sixty years ago," Gran said, "and I was ten, and I was called Willa. Your great-grandfather was the tollkeeper on this very bridge. He collected nothing, because nobody paid. They thought it was a joke. I thought it was my fault."

She tucked the button into her sleeve. "I had no friends. I was new, and strange, and I smelled of river mud. The Bridge Club dared me, just as they dared you. To cross the old bridge at dusk. To see if I was brave enough to go under the arch."

Rue felt the air leave the room. "You went?"

"I went," Gran said. "I was very small, and very scared. And when I crouched down, I saw him. He was not as large as he is now. He was only a hundred and forty. He was sitting with his knees drawn up, weeping because he had lost a shoe. It was a very pretty shoe. I have kept it, though I cannot find it."
pages.image: An elderly woman with silver bun and half-moon glasses stands in a dim room, holding a large wooden button, her expression solemn and thoughtful, with a small bedside table and a lamp in the background.

pages.text:
"He was lonely, Willa. Or rather, I was. And so I sat down. And I paid the toll. I told him about the school, and the bad tea, and the boy who stepped on my cat. He listened. He is a good listener."

Gran smiled, a small, fragile thing. "We were friends for a whole summer. I came every day. I told him stories, and he told me about the moss. He taught me how to coax it into shapes. I showed him how to make a good scone. He gave me this button. A horn button from his waistcoat. He said it was so I would always have a piece of him, should I ever feel the need for a very heavy paperweight."

Rue looked at the button. It was dark and smooth, and it sat in the blue cloth like a sleeping eye.

"He was young," Gran said. "He was still learning how to be a troll. He was shy, and he was polite, and he sang badly. Just like now."
pages.image: A memory scene of a small girl and a young mossy troll sitting together under a stone arch, sharing a meal of scones, the troll wearing a patched waistcoat and round spectacles, looking gentle and shy.

pages.text:
"But then I turned thirteen. The older girls, the ones who actually had friends, decided to go to a picnic on the Founders' Green. I had waited years to be asked, and I was wearing my best dress. While I was picking my teeth, one of them, Mrs. Tanner before she was a Tanner, saw the button in my pocket."

Gran’s voice dropped. "She asked what it was. I should have told her. I should have said it was a promise. But I looked at her, and then I looked at the others, and I saw the way they looked at me. I saw the door closing. And I laughed."

"I said, 'Oh, that’s just a button. I found it under the bridge. Yes, I know about the troll. I’ve even seen him. He’s quite friendly. He cried once. I made him cry, actually. I told him his shoes were ugly.'"

The room was very quiet, holding its breath. Rue could hear the tick of the clock on the mantelpiece, a steady, wooden heartbeat in the silence that followed.
pages.image: A tense scene in a sunlit yard where a group of older girls look at a young girl with a surprised, guilty expression, one girl reaching for a large wooden button visible in the young girl's pocket.

pages.text:
"The town did not hunt him then. The story was too silly to believe. They thought I was making it up. But Hobb heard it. Word travels under bridges. He asked me why. I stood there, and I said I was sorry. I said I had been a coward. I said I wanted to be like them."

Gran wiped her eyes with her sleeve. "And he said, 'Then you will never come back.' And he was right. I have spent sixty years not going back. I have spent sixty years not forgiving myself. I look at this button every year on the day of the Founders' Fair, and I remember the sound of his voice. It is a sound that is quieter than a whisper, but it is louder than the town."

Rue felt a cold weight in her chest. "You could have told them," she said softly. "You could have told them he was kind."

Gran shook her head. "I was afraid. I was afraid of being strange. I was afraid of being alone. And so I chose to be part of the group. And I lost the friend under the bridge. I have carried that button ever since."
pages.image: An elderly woman sitting alone at a window, holding a large wooden button in her hands, looking out at a rainy street with a distant view of a stone bridge, her face filled with regret and sadness.

pages.text:
Rue held the button in her lap, feeling the grain of the wood beneath her fingers. It was warm, as if it remembered the heat of the troll’s hand, and it sat heavy and solid in her palm.

"He said sorry doesn't put him back where he was," Rue said finally. Her voice was small, but it did not shake.

Gran looked at her, and for the first time in a long while, her face was just a face. "He is right," she said. "But it took me sixty years to learn that saying it anyway is not the same as asking to be let off. I did not ask to be let off. I asked to be remembered."

She placed the button in Rue’s open hand and closed her fingers gently around it.

"Don't make him forgive you," Gran said. "That is not your job. Make sure he is still got somewhere to go, if he does. Make sure the bridge is held up. That is all any of us can do."

Rue looked down at the button. It was not a paperweight. It was a key. And she knew, with a sudden, clear certainty, where she had to go.
pages.image: A close-up of a young girl's hands holding a large, dark wooden button, her expression serious and determined, with the blurred background of a warm, cluttered room, symbolizing a new resolve.
